guide.title: Bozrah, Connecticut: A Biblical Name and Three Mill Villages
guide.intro: Bozrah began as part of Norwich's original nine-miles-square grant, in the section known as the Parish of West Farms; it split off as its own parish in 1737 and was incorporated as a separate town in 1786. Its odd biblical name comes from a legend: residents wanted to call the place "Bath," but a Hartford legislator, amused by a delegate's parti-colored homespun clothing, quoted Isaiah 63:1 — "Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?" — and the General Assembly adopted Bozrah instead. The town is really three villages: Fitchville, the center; Leffingwell, a Route 82 crossroads; and Gilman, a mill village. Early residents farmed corn, oats and flax while the Yantic River powered cotton manufactories, and the Palmer Brothers ran the Fitchville Mills for roughly a century. Reuben Hyde Walworth, nominated three times to the U.S. Supreme Court, was born here in 1788.

sections.heading: Fitchville, Leffingwell and Gilman
sections.body: Bozrah began as part of Norwich's nine-miles-square grant, in the Parish of West Farms; it became its own parish in 1737 and was incorporated as a separate town in 1786, taking its biblical name after a Hartford legislator, amused by a delegate's parti-colored homespun clothing, quoted Isaiah 63:1 rather than approve the requested name "Bath." The town is really three villages — Fitchville, the center; Leffingwell, a Route 82 crossroads; and Gilman, a mill village on Fitchville Road. Early residents farmed corn, oats and flax while the Yantic River powered cotton manufactories in the Fitchville and Bozrahville sections, and the Palmer Brothers ran the Fitchville Mills for roughly a century; their mill houses and stone buildings still stand and remain in use. Reuben Hyde Walworth, born here in 1788, was nominated three times to the U.S. Supreme Court by President Tyler in 1844, though the Senate never voted on any of the nominations. Bozrah covers 20.2 square miles with 2,429 residents at the 2020 census, bordered by Norwich, Montville, Salem, Colchester, Lebanon and Franklin, with 529-acre Gardner Lake reaching into its southwestern corner — though the lake's developed beach and boat launch sit across the line in Salem.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body: Bozrah is a drive-to town with no rail service of its own: take Route 2, the Norwich-Hartford expressway that runs straight through town, to Exit 33 (renumbered from the old Exit 23 in Connecticut's 2025 milepost conversion) for Route 163 and Fitchville, or approach the Leffingwell crossroads on Route 82, with I-395 meeting Route 2 just east in Norwich. The nearest passenger trains are Amtrak Northeast Regional and CTrail Shore Line East at New London Union Station, roughly 15 miles south — Acela no longer stops there — where you will still need a car for the rest of the trip. No passenger rail station exists in Bozrah or in any of its bordering towns.

sections.heading: Maples Farm Park and Odetah's mini golf
sections.body: Maples Farm Park, a nineteenth-century farmhouse and 32 acres the town acquired in 2007, has four hiking loops totaling 3.5 miles open to horseback riding, plus an outdoor pavilion and the Bozrah Farmers Market on Fridays in season. The Glemboski-Ous Preserve, protected by the Avalonia Land Conservancy in 2024, straddles the Bozrah-Montville line with about 3.5 miles of trail through forest and wetland — terrain is moderate to difficult, stream crossings are unbridged, and bow hunting is permitted in season, so wear blaze orange in the fall. For an afternoon out, Odetah Camping Resort's Knolls & Holes miniature golf course has 18 holes with water hazards and sand traps, and the resort's Oasis Lakeside Cafe is the only sit-down food service verified inside Bozrah itself; Acorn Acres Campground, open year-round, is the town's other camping option.

faq.question: How do I get to Bozrah?
faq.answer: By car — Route 2 runs straight through town; take Exit 33 (Route 163 south / Haughton Road, renumbered from the old Exit 23 in 2025) for Fitchville, or reach the Leffingwell crossroads via Route 82. There is no passenger rail station anywhere in Bozrah.

faq.question: Is there a train to Bozrah?
faq.answer: No. Shore Line East's nine stations run only between New Haven and New London, and no branch reaches Bozrah or any of its bordering towns. The nearest station is New London Union Station, roughly 15 miles south.

faq.question: Why is the town called Bozrah?
faq.answer: By legend, residents wanted to name the settlement "Bath" after the English spa town, but a Hartford legislator, amused by a delegate's parti-colored homespun clothing, quoted the Book of Isaiah's line about "dyed garments from Bozrah" and the General Assembly adopted that name instead in 1786.

faq.question: Is there a restaurant in Bozrah?
faq.answer: The Oasis Lakeside Cafe at Odetah Camping Resort is the only sit-down food service that could be verified inside Bozrah. Call ahead, since hours and walk-in access for non-campers are not published.

faq.question: Is there a hotel in Bozrah?
faq.answer: No hotel, inn or B&B could be verified inside Bozrah. The only verified overnight lodging is camping-style, at Odetah Camping Resort (cabins, yurts, RV and tent sites) and Acorn Acres Campground, open year-round.

faq.question: What is Maples Farm Park?
faq.answer: A town park built around a nineteenth-century farmhouse and 32 acres acquired in 2007, with four hiking loops totaling 3.5 miles open to horseback riding, an outdoor pavilion, and the Bozrah Farmers Market on Fridays in season.

places.name: Maples Farm Park
places.summary: A nineteenth-century farmhouse and 32 acres the Town of Bozrah acquired in April 2007. Four hiking loops total 3.5 miles and are also open to horseback riding, alongside a historic Homestead and an outdoor pavilion available for event rental.

places.name: Glemboski-Ous Preserve
places.summary: A 159.42-acre Avalonia Land Conservancy preserve straddling the Bozrah-Montville line, protected in 2024, with about 3.5 miles of trail through forest, wetland and a vernal pool. Terrain is moderate to difficult, some stream crossings are still unbridged, and bow hunting is permitted in season — wear blaze orange in the fall. Open dawn to dusk, dogs on leash.

places.name: Bozrah Farmers Market
places.summary: Held Fridays 4-7 p.m. in season on the grounds of Maples Farm Park, with locally grown produce, homemade treats, handcrafted goods, live music and family activities. Confirm current-season opening and closing dates before visiting.

places.name: Knolls & Holes Miniature Golf at Odetah
places.summary: An 18-hole championship-style mini golf course at Odetah Camping Resort, with water hazards, sand traps and steep course contours. A round is $10 per person; clubs are available at the Scoop Shack, or the main office when the Scoop Shack is closed.

places.name: The Oasis Lakeside Cafe
places.summary: Odetah Camping Resort's lakeside food-and-fun venue, serving breakfast, lunch and dinner with a deck over the beach and lake and evening live music; during off-peak camping season it is open weekends only. No other sit-down restaurant could be verified in Bozrah — call (800) 448-1193 before driving out.

places.name: Odetah Camping Resort
places.summary: A camping resort with standard, deluxe and premier cabins plus yurts alongside RV, safari and tent sites; premier cabins carry a seven-night minimum in summer, and standard and deluxe units do not include linens, dishes or cookware. No conventional hotel, inn or B&B could be verified inside Bozrah.

places.name: Acorn Acres Campground
places.summary: A year-round campground on 100 wooded acres with over 200 sites plus four- and six-person air-conditioned cabins. Phone (860) 859-1020 to confirm rates and availability.
